chapters.title: Chapter 6: Risk Parity and Volatility-Weighted Allocation

lessons.title: Why Equal Capital Allocation Is Not Equal Risk Allocation

body.text: Chapter 3 proved, with actual numbers, that a 25% capital weight in four assets does not mean 25% of the risk in any of them. This chapter takes that finding and turns it into an actual portfolio construction methodology, risk parity, built specifically to correct it, rather than a fact you simply have to live with.

children.text: Chapter 3's closing lesson showed a 25% capital weight in Nifty producing nearly 60% of an illustrative portfolio's total risk. This chapter builds the fix properly: what risk parity actually targets, why it is a genuinely different design choice from mean-variance optimization, and how it relates to the vol-scaling this course has already used, informally, throughout Chapters 4 and 5.
Three Ways to Allocate Capital, and What Each One Actually Optimizes For

cells: Lets the highest-volatility asset dominate total risk
Maximum expected return per unit of risk
Extremely sensitive to expected return estimation error
Volatilities and correlations only, no expected returns
Can require leverage to hit a target return; more on this in Lesson 4

children.text: Why Not Just Use Mean-Variance Optimization? The Expected Return Problem

Classical Markowitz mean-variance optimization is the textbook answer to portfolio construction, and it needs three inputs: expected returns, volatilities, and correlations. Volatilities and correlations, this course's entire Chapter 3, can be estimated reasonably well from historical data. Expected returns cannot. Small errors in expected return estimates get amplified disproportionately by the optimizer, a well-documented problem in portfolio theory sometimes described as error maximization, since the optimizer tends to load heavily onto whichever asset's expected return estimate happens to look best, precisely the assets whose estimates are least reliable.

body.text: Risk parity's real appeal is not that it is mathematically superior to mean-variance optimization in every sense, it is that it deliberately avoids needing the one input, expected returns, that nobody can reliably forecast. It builds a portfolio entirely from the inputs this course's Chapter 3 spent real effort learning to estimate properly, volatility and correlation, and asks nothing else of you.

children.text: Formally Defining Risk Parity: Equal Marginal Risk Contribution

Chapter 3 defined each asset's risk contribution as its weight multiplied by the covariance-weighted sum of its relationship with the rest of the portfolio. Risk parity takes that same quantity and turns it from a diagnostic into an explicit target: find the set of weights such that every asset's risk contribution is equal.

body.latex: RC_i = w_i (\Sigma w)_i, \quad \text{target: } RC_i = RC_j = \frac{\sigma_p^2}{N} \; \forall i,j
body.caption: Risk parity's defining condition. Every asset's risk contribution, RC_i, should equal every other asset's, each contributing an equal 1/N share of total portfolio variance. Chapter 3's equal-weight example violated this badly; risk parity solves directly for the weights that satisfy it.

children.text: A Simplified Special Case: Inverse Volatility Weighting

Solving the full risk parity condition exactly, accounting for every pairwise correlation, generally requires numerical optimization, which Lesson 3 builds properly. A widely used, simpler approximation ignores cross-correlation effects and weights each asset inversely to its own volatility, exactly the vol-scaling formula this course has already used informally throughout Chapters 4 and 5 for individual position sizing. Applied at the whole-portfolio level, using this course's four core instruments, inverse volatility weighting looks like this.

body.caption: Inverse Volatility Weights vs Equal Capital Weighting, Same Four Assets as Chapter 3

children.text: This is a genuine improvement over equal capital weighting, but it is not yet true risk parity, since it ignores the off-diagonal correlation terms this course spent an entire chapter building tools to measure. Lesson 3 solves the full version, incorporating the actual covariance matrix, and shows exactly how much it differs from this simplified inverse-vol approximation.

Lesson 2 covers volatility targeting and rebalancing mechanics in more depth. Lesson 3 builds a full, correlation-aware risk parity portfolio across Nifty, Gold, and G-Secs as a concrete case study, reusing Chapter 3's actual covariance matrix. Lesson 4 covers risk parity's genuine weakness honestly: the leverage it often requires, and how that exposure behaved specifically during 2022's rate-hike cycle, this course's recurring example of a regime that breaks conventional diversification assumptions.

body.title: "We Already Do Risk Parity"
body.scenario: A desk head tells an investment committee that their multi-asset book already runs risk parity, pointing out that every individual position across Nifty, Gold, G-Sec futures, and USD-INR is vol-scaled using the target-volatility-divided-by-realized-volatility formula from Chapter 4. A committee member familiar with this lesson pushes back, asking whether this is actually true risk parity or something else.
body.prompt: Is the desk head's claim accurate? What is the actual gap between what they described and true risk parity?
body.modelAnswer: The desk head's approach is the inverse-volatility approximation covered in this lesson, a genuine improvement over equal capital weighting, but not true risk parity. Vol-scaling each individual position ignores the correlations between those positions, exactly the off-diagonal covariance terms Chapter 3 spent an entire chapter building tools to measure. True risk parity requires that every asset's risk contribution, which depends on its covariance with every other asset in the book, not just its own volatility, be equalized, a condition the inverse-vol approximation only satisfies exactly when all pairwise correlations happen to be zero. The gap between the two approaches is precisely what Lesson 3 quantifies by building the fully correlation-aware version.

body.title: Computing an Inverse-Volatility Weight
body.prompt: Using inverse-volatility weighting (ignoring correlation) on the four core assets (Nifty 20%, Gold 12%, G-Sec Futures 6%, USD-INR 7% volatility), what normalized weight does G-Sec Futures receive, so that all four weights sum to 100%? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Inverse volatilities: 1/20=0.050, 1/12=0.083, 1/6=0.167, 1/7=0.143, summing to 0.443. G-Sec Futures' share is 0.167/0.443 ≈ 0.376, or 37.6%, by far the largest weight of the four, since it is by far the least volatile instrument in the book.

body.title: The Core Practical Advantage of Risk Parity
body.question: Based on this lesson, what is risk parity's main practical advantage over mean-variance optimization?
options: Risk parity always produces higher returns than mean-variance optimization
Risk parity does not require estimating expected returns, which are notoriously unreliable to forecast, relying instead only on volatility and correlation
Risk parity requires no historical data of any kind
Risk parity is only usable for equity portfolios
body.explanation: Mean-variance optimization requires expected return estimates, which are highly unreliable and can be amplified into large, unstable position sizes by the optimizer. Risk parity sidesteps this entirely, building its allocation only from volatility and correlation, the two inputs this course's Chapter 3 already built genuine tools to estimate.

points: Equal capital weighting, mean-variance optimization, and risk parity target genuinely different things and require genuinely different inputs
Mean-variance optimization's biggest practical weakness is its extreme sensitivity to expected return estimation error, a well-documented problem in portfolio theory
Risk parity's core appeal is that it never requires expected return estimates, relying only on volatility and correlation, exactly what Chapter 3 built tools to measure
Risk parity's formal target is equal marginal risk contribution across every asset, RC_i equal for all i, not equal capital weight

Inverse-volatility weighting is a simplified approximation of risk parity that ignores correlation; on this course's four core assets it shifts weight heavily toward G-Sec Futures and USD-INR, away from Nifty
True, fully correlation-aware risk parity requires solving for weights numerically, which Lesson 3 builds directly on Chapter 3's actual covariance matrix
